items.title: Python Intro and Download
explanation: Python is a popular programming language used to write instructions that tell a computer what to do.
Simple Definition: Python is a high-level, general-purpose programming language known for its simple and readable syntax.
Python can be used in many different areas of software development. The same programming language can be used for small automation scripts as well as large applications and data processing systems.
Python ↓ Write Instructions ↓ Computer Executes Them ↓ Perform a Task
Python Uses Python ├── Automation & Scripting ├── Data Analysis ├── Data Engineering ⭐ ├── Web Development ├── Machine Learning ├── Artificial Intelligence └── Application Development
Why Python Is Important for Data Engineering ⭐
Python is widely used in Data Engineering because it is useful for writing scripts, processing data, automating repetitive tasks, connecting to databases, calling APIs, and building data pipelines.
Data Engineering Workflow Get Data ↓ Process Data ↓ Transform Data ↓ Store Data ↓ Automate Pipeline Python can be used in many of these steps ⭐
Later in this roadmap, you will use Python with tools and libraries for working with data. For now, the goal is to first build a strong understanding of core Python.
Important: Do not try to learn every Python library immediately. First understand Python fundamentals such as variables, conditions, loops, functions, collections, files, exceptions, and modules.
Python is known for having syntax that is relatively easy to read and write. Python code often looks closer to plain English than many other programming languages.
This instruction tells Python to display the text:
Even without knowing Python, it is easy to understand the general purpose of this code.
Python treats uppercase and lowercase letters differently.
print → Valid Python built-in function Print → Different name ❌
Remember: In Python, print, Print, and PRINT are treated as different names.
A programming language provides rules and syntax that allow developers to write instructions for computers.
Developer ↓ Writes Python Code ↓ Python Processes the Code ↓ Computer Performs the Instructions
Python is called a high-level language because developers can write code using human-readable syntax without directly managing many low-level computer operations.
High-Level Developer writes: print("Hello") ↓ Python handles many lower-level details ↓ Computer executes the instruction
As a beginner, you do not need to understand the internal low-level details immediately. Focus first on learning how to write and understand Python code.
A general-purpose programming language can be used for many different types of applications instead of being designed for only one specific purpose.
Python One Language ↓ Many Uses Automation Data Web AI Applications
In this roadmap, Python is not being learned only for writing small programs. It will become one of the core languages you use throughout your Data Engineering journey.
Foundation Git & GitHub ↓ Python ⭐ ↓ SQL ↓ Linux / Command Line ↓ Database Fundamentals ──────────────────── Later NumPy Pandas APIs Data Pipelines Airflow Spark PySpark Projects
This is why understanding the fundamentals properly is important before moving to libraries such as NumPy, Pandas, or PySpark.
Python has different versions. For modern development, you should learn and use a supported Python 3 version.
Older Python Versions ↓ Python 2 ❌ Modern Python Development ↓ Python 3 ⭐
Rule: For this roadmap, use Python 3. The exact minor version may change over time, but the concepts you learn will remain largely the same.
Python should be downloaded from the official Python website.
Download a current supported Python 3 release appropriate for your operating system.
Official Python Website ↓ Downloads ↓ Choose Your Operating System ↓ Download Python 3 ↓ Run Installer
Follow these general steps when installing Python on Windows:

Step 1 Open the official Python download page ↓ Step 2 Download Python for Windows ↓ Step 3 Run the installer ↓ Step 4 Enable Add Python to PATH ⭐ ↓ Step 5 Install Python ↓ Step 6 Verify the installation
During installation, you may see an option similar to Add Python to PATH. Enabling this allows you to run Python from the command line without manually entering the full installation location.
Without PATH Need Python's Full Location ↓ C:\...\Python\python.exe ──────────────────── With Python Added to PATH ⭐ Open Terminal ↓ python ↓ Python Runs
Important: When installing Python, make sure you understand whether Python has been added to your system PATH. This makes using Python from the command line much easier.
How to Check Whether Python Is Installed
After installation, open Command Prompt or a terminal and run:
On some Windows systems, you can also use:
Terminal ↓ python --version ↓ Python 3.x.x ↓ Python Installed Successfully ✅
What If the python Command Does Not Work?
If the command is not recognized, Python may not be installed correctly or its installation location may not be available through PATH.
If Python is still not found, check the installation and PATH configuration, then reopen the terminal after making changes.
Tip: After installing Python or changing PATH settings, close and reopen Command Prompt or your terminal before testing the command again.
Installing Python gives your computer the Python interpreter needed to run Python code. A code editor is a separate tool used to write and manage your code more comfortably.
Python Installation ↓ Provides Python Interpreter ↓ Runs Python Code ──────────────────── Code Editor ↓ Helps You Write Code ↓ Edit / Organize / Run Code
You will learn more about writing and running Python code in the next topic.

Mistake 1 ❌ Download Python from an unknown website Correct ✅ Use the official Python website ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Install an outdated or unsupported version without checking Correct ✅ Use a supported Python 3 version ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Forget about PATH and wonder why the python command does not work Correct ✅ Check the installation and PATH configuration ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Think Python installation and a code editor are the same thing Correct ✅ Python runs the code; an editor helps you write it ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ Jump immediately into Pandas or PySpark Correct ✅ Build strong Python fundamentals first ⭐
Python = Programming Language Python 3 = Learn This ⭐ Official Website ↓ Download ↓ Install ↓ Check PATH ↓ Verify with python --version ↓ Start Learning Python

ConceptMeaning
PythonA high-level, general-purpose programming language
Python 3The modern version family you should learn
High-levelAllows developers to write more human-readable code
General-purposeCan be used for many types of applications
PATHHelps the operating system find Python from the command line
python --versionChecks the installed Python version
py --versionAlternative command commonly available on Windows
Python interpreterRuns Python code

Final Definition: Python is a high-level, general-purpose programming language known for its readable syntax. It is widely used for automation, data processing, Data Engineering, web development, AI, and many other applications. Install a supported Python 3 version, verify it from the command line, and then begin learning the core language fundamentals.
practice: Step 1: Open the official Python website and go to the Downloads section.
https://www.python.org/downloads/
Step 2: Download a supported Python 3 installer for your operating system.
Step 3: Run the installer and check the available installation options.
Step 4: Make sure Python is available from your command line, including checking the Add Python to PATH option when applicable.
Step 5: Complete the Python installation.
Step 6: Open Command Prompt or a terminal.
Step 7: Check the Python version.
python --version
Step 8: If needed on Windows, also try:
py --version
Step 9: Confirm that the output shows a Python 3 version.
Step 10: Type the following command and observe whether Python starts interactively:
python
Step 11: When finished, exit the Python interactive environment.
exit()
Final Understanding Check:

1. What is Python? 2. Why is Python useful for Data Engineering? 3. What does high-level mean? 4. What does general-purpose mean? 5. Which major Python version should you learn? 6. Where should you download Python from? 7. Why is PATH useful? 8. Which command checks the Python version? 9. What is the difference between Python and a code editor? 10. Complete: Download → Install → ______ → Start Learning
Practice Goal: You should be able to explain what Python is, why it is useful for Data Engineering, install a supported Python 3 version, and verify that Python is available from your command line.

items.title: Python Interpreter and Running Python Code
explanation: The Python interpreter is the program that reads and executes Python code.
Simple Definition: The Python interpreter is software that reads Python instructions and executes them so the computer can perform the requested task.
When you write Python code, the computer does not directly understand your Python syntax. The Python interpreter processes your code and executes the instructions.
You ↓ Write Python Code ↓ Python Interpreter ↓ Processes Instructions ↓ Computer Performs the Task ↓ Output
When this code runs, the Python interpreter executes the print() instruction and produces:
Think of the Interpreter as a Translator
A simple way to understand the interpreter is to think of it as something between your Python code and the computer.
Your Instruction print("Hello") ↓ Python Interpreter Understands Python Instructions ↓ Computer Executes the Required Operations ↓ Hello
Remember: You write Python code. The Python interpreter runs that code.
What Happens When You Run a Python File?
A Python program is commonly saved with the .py file extension.
hello.py ↓ Contains Python Code ↓ Python Interpreter Reads File ↓ Executes print() ↓ Hello, World!
You can start Python directly from a terminal and execute code one instruction at a time. This is called the interactive Python environment.
Open Command Prompt or a terminal and run:
On some Windows systems, you may use:
If Python starts successfully, you will see information about the Python version followed by:
The >>> prompt means Python is ready to accept a command.
Terminal ↓ python ↓ Python Starts ↓ >>> ↓ Type Python Code ↓ Press Enter ↓ See Result
In interactive mode, Python reads your instruction, executes it immediately, and usually shows the result.
Best Use: Interactive mode is useful for quickly testing Python code, checking small expressions, and experimenting with concepts.
To exit the Python interactive environment, type:
Python Interactive Mode >>> ↓ exit() ↓ Back to Terminal
For real programs, you normally write code in a file and save it with the .py extension.
Open a terminal in the folder containing the file and run:
hello.py ↓ python hello.py ↓ Python Interpreter Opens File ↓ Reads Code ↓ Executes Code ↓ Output Appears
python ↓ Start Python Interpreter hello.py ↓ File Python Should Run
Meaning: Use the Python interpreter to run the code stored inside hello.py.
When running a Python file from the terminal, the terminal needs to know where the file is located.
You can first move to that folder:
Terminal Current Folder C:\Projects\Python ↓ hello.py Exists Here ↓ python hello.py ↓ Program Runs ✅
You will learn command-line navigation in more detail in the Linux / Command Line section of this roadmap.
You can also write and run Python programs using a code editor or IDE. The editor provides features such as syntax highlighting, file management, debugging, and easier code organization.
Code Editor / IDE ↓ Write Python Code ↓ Save as .py File ↓ Run ↓ Python Interpreter Executes Code ↓ Output
Important: A code editor helps you write code, but the Python interpreter is responsible for executing Python code.

Interactive ModePython File
Run code one command at a timeRun a saved program
Useful for quick testingUseful for real programs
Uses the >>> promptUses a .py file
Code is typed directly into PythonCode is written and saved in a file
Good for experimentationGood for reusable programs
These two concepts are different and beginners sometimes confuse them.
Terminal / Command Prompt ↓ A place where you type system commands Example: python hello.py ──────────────────── Python Interpreter ↓ The program that executes Python code Example: print("Hello")
You can use a terminal to start the Python interpreter.
Terminal ↓ Type: python ↓ Python Interpreter Starts ↓ >>> ↓ Run Python Commands
For simple programs, Python generally executes statements from top to bottom in the order they are reached.
Line 1 → Step 1 ↓ Line 2 → Step 2 ↓ Line 3 → Step 3
Later, conditions, loops, functions, and other concepts can change the normal flow of execution.

Mistake 1 ❌ Think Python and the terminal are the same thing Correct ✅ The terminal can be used to start Python ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Save a Python program without .py Correct ✅ Use a .py extension Example: hello.py ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Run python wrong_file.py from a folder where the file does not exist Correct ✅ Check your current folder or provide the correct file path ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Think the code editor itself is Python Correct ✅ The editor helps write code; Python executes it ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ Forget to save changes before running the file Correct ✅ Save the file, then run it again
Write Code ↓ Save as .py ↓ Python Interpreter Runs It ↓ See Output Quick Test? ↓ Use Interactive Mode Real Program? ↓ Use a .py File ⭐

ConceptMeaning
Python InterpreterProgram that reads and executes Python code
Interactive ModeRun Python commands one at a time using the Python prompt
>>>Python is ready to accept an interactive command
.pyCommon file extension for Python programs
pythonStarts the Python interpreter
python file.pyRuns a Python file
exit()Exits the Python interactive environment
TerminalInterface where commands can be entered

Final Definition: The Python interpreter is the software that reads and executes Python code. You can run Python interactively for quick experiments or save your code in a .py file and run it using commands such as python filename.py.

Step 2: Start the Python interpreter.

Step 10: Open the terminal in the folder containing hello.py.
Step 11: Run the file:

Step 12: Change the text inside the file, save it, and run the command again.

qna.a: The Python interpreter is software that reads and executes Python code.

qna.q: Q2. What happens when you run Python code?
qna.a: The Python interpreter reads the instructions and executes the required operations.

qna.q: Q3. What is interactive mode?
qna.a: Interactive mode allows you to enter and run Python instructions one at a time directly in the Python environment.

qna.q: Q4. What does the >>> prompt mean?
qna.a: It means the Python interpreter is running and ready to accept a command.

qna.q: Q5. How can you start the Python interpreter?
qna.a: You can commonly use the command python, or py on some Windows systems.

qna.q: Q6. How do you exit the Python interactive environment?
qna.a: You can type exit() and press Enter.

qna.q: Q7. What file extension is commonly used for Python programs?
qna.a: The .py extension.

qna.q: Q8. How do you run a Python file named hello.py?
qna.a: Use the command: python hello.py

qna.q: Q9. What does python hello.py mean?
qna.a: It means use the Python interpreter to execute the code stored in the hello.py file.

qna.q: Q10. What is the difference between interactive mode and running a Python file?
qna.a: Interactive mode is useful for running commands quickly one at a time, while a Python file is used to save and run a complete program.

qna.q: Q11. Is a terminal the same as the Python interpreter?
qna.a: No. A terminal is an interface for entering commands, while the Python interpreter is software that executes Python code.

qna.q: Q12. Is a code editor the same as Python?
qna.a: No. A code editor helps you write and organize code, while the Python interpreter executes the code.

qna.q: Q13. Why does the current folder matter when running python hello.py?
qna.a: Python needs to be able to find the specified file. If the file is not in the current folder, you need the correct path.

qna.q: Q14. In what order does simple Python code normally execute?
qna.a: Simple Python statements normally execute from top to bottom in the order they are reached.

items.title: `print()`
explanation: The print() function is used to display output on the screen.
Simple Definition: print() is a built-in Python function used to display values, text, and other information as output.
The most common example is printing text:
Python Code print("Hello, World!") ↓ Python Interpreter Executes print() ↓ Output Screen Hello, World!
print() is one of Python's built-in functions, meaning it is available without importing anything. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}
print ↓ Function Name ( ↓ Opening Parenthesis "Hello" ↓ Value to Display ) ↓ Closing Parenthesis
In simple terms, you put the value you want to display inside the parentheses.
Memory Rule: print(value) → Display the value as output.
Text in Python is written inside quotes. This type of value is called a string.
print("Python") ↓ Displays ↓ Python print('Python') ↓ Displays ↓ Python
Both single quotes and double quotes can be used for normal string values.
You do not put quotes around a number when you want Python to treat it as a numeric value.
Important: The output may look the same, but 100 and "100" are different types of values.
You can place an expression inside print(). Python evaluates the expression and displays the result.
You can provide multiple values to print() by separating them with commas.
By default, print() separates multiple values with a space.
print("Python", "SQL", "Git") ↓ Values are separated by commas ↓ Python SQL Git
The sep parameter controls what is placed between multiple values. The default separator is a space.
Values Python SQL Git ↓ Separator = " | " ↓ Python | SQL | Git
By default, each print() call ends with a new line. The next output starts on the next line.
First print() ↓ First ↓ New Line Second print() ↓ Second ↓ New Line Third print() ↓ Third
The end parameter controls what is added after the printed output. By default, Python ends print() with a new line.
Here, the first print() ends with a space instead of moving to a new line.
Default print("A") print("B") Output: A B ──────────────────── Custom end print("A", end="-") print("B") Output: A-B
Sometimes you want to display quotation marks as part of the text.
You can also use an escape character when needed:
Note: You will learn strings in more detail later. For now, understand that quotes tell Python that you are working with text.
Later, you will store values in variables. You can then use print() to display those values.
name = "Nani" ↓ Variable stores value ↓ print(name) ↓ Displays stored value ↓ Nani
print(name) ↓ Displays the value stored in name ──────────────────── print("name") ↓ Displays the text name
In real programs, print() can help you quickly check values while learning or debugging code.
print("Starting data pipeline") print("Reading source data") print("Processing completed")
Starting data pipeline Reading source data Processing completed
For production applications, structured logging is usually more appropriate than relying only on print(). You will learn logging later in this roadmap.
For Now: Use print() to understand your code, display results, and quickly inspect values while learning Python.
This works because print is the correct built-in function name.
This causes an error because Print is treated as a different name.
print() → Correct ✅ Print() → Different name ❌ PRINT() → Different name ❌
In Python 3, print is called like a function, so parentheses are required.
Rule: Always use print() with parentheses when calling the function.

Mistake 1 ❌ Print("Hello") Correct ✅ print("Hello") ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ print "Hello" Correct ✅ print("Hello") ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ print(Hello) Correct ✅ print("Hello") Without quotes, Python looks for a variable named Hello. ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Expect multiple print() calls to appear on one line Correct ✅ Understand that print() adds a new line by default. Use end= when needed. ──────────────────── Mistake 5 ❌ Confuse print(name) with print("name") Correct ✅ print(name) → variable value print("name") → text
Want to Display Something? ↓ Use print() Text ↓ print("Hello") Number ↓ print(100) Calculation ↓ print(10 + 20) Multiple Values ↓ print("Python", "SQL")

ConceptMeaning
print()Displays output
TextUsually written inside quotes
NumberCan be printed directly without quotes
Multiple valuesSeparate values with commas
sepControls the separator between values
endControls what appears after the output
Default behaviorEnds output with a new line

Final Definition: print() is a built-in Python function used to display output. It can print text, numbers, calculations, variables, and multiple values. By default, it separates multiple values with spaces and ends each call with a new line. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}

1. What does print() do? 2. Is print() a built-in function? 3. How do you print text? 4. How do you print a number? 5. What is the difference between 100 and "100"? 6. What does sep control? 7. What does end control? 8. What happens by default after print() displays output? 9. What is the difference between print(name) and print("name")? 10. Which is correct? print() or Print()?
Practice Goal: You should be able to use print() to display text, numbers, calculations, variables, and multiple values, including using the basic sep and end parameters.

qna.q: Q1. What is print() in Python?
qna.a: print() is a built-in Python function used to display output.

qna.q: Q2. How do you print Hello?
qna.a: print("Hello")

qna.q: Q3. Can print() display numbers?
qna.a: Yes. For example: print(100)

qna.q: Q4. Can print() display the result of a calculation?
qna.a: Yes. For example, print(10 + 20) displays 30.

qna.q: Q5. How can you print multiple values?
qna.a: Pass the values to print() separated by commas, for example: print("Python", "SQL").

qna.q: Q6. What is the default separator between multiple values in print()?
qna.a: A space.

qna.q: Q7. What does the sep parameter do?
qna.a: It controls the separator placed between multiple values.

qna.q: Q8. What does the end parameter do?
qna.a: It controls what is added after the printed output.

qna.q: Q9. What happens by default after print() runs?
qna.a: The next output starts on a new line.

qna.q: Q10. Is Python case-sensitive for print()?
qna.a: Yes. print() is different from Print() and PRINT().

qna.q: Q11. Are parentheses required when calling print() in Python 3?
qna.a: Yes. Use syntax such as print("Hello").

qna.a: print(name) displays the value stored in the variable name, while print("name") displays the text name.

qna.a: print("Python", "SQL", "Git", sep="-")

items.title: `input()`
explanation: The input() function is used to take input from the user while a Python program is running.
Simple Definition: input() is a built-in Python function that waits for the user to enter a value and returns that value to the program.
Python Program Starts ↓ input() Displays a Prompt ↓ Enter your name: ↓ User Types: Nani ↓ Press Enter ↓ input() Returns "Nani" ↓ Value Stored in name
input ↓ Built-in Function ( ↓ Opening Parenthesis "Enter your name: " ↓ Prompt Shown to User ) ↓ Closing Parenthesis
The text inside input() is optional. It is commonly used to tell the user what information they should enter.
A very important concept is that input() returns user input as a string by default.
Memory Rule: input() → User enters data → Python receives it as a str by default.
Because input() returns a string, you need type conversion when you want to perform numeric calculations.
This causes an error because Python cannot directly add a string and an integer.
User Enters 25 ↓ input() ↓ "25" → String ↓ int() ↓ 25 → Integer ↓ 25 + 5 ↓ 30
Use int() when the user should enter a whole number.
If the user enters 5, the output is:
Use float() when the user may enter a decimal number.
Normally, the value returned by input() is stored in a variable.
city = input("Enter your city: ") print("You live in", city)
input() ↓ Gets user value ↓ Store in variable ↓ Use variable later Example: city = input(...) ↓ city stores user input
You can call input() without any text inside it.
However, using a prompt usually makes the program easier for users to understand.
Good Practice: Use a clear prompt so the user knows what information they should enter.
You can call input() multiple times to collect different values.
name = input("Enter your name: ") age = input("Enter your age: ") city = input("Enter your city: ") print(name) print(age) print(city)
Program ↓ Input 1 → Name ↓ Input 2 → Age ↓ Input 3 → City ↓ Values stored in variables ↓ Use the values
name = input("Enter your name: ") print("Hello", name)
input() ↓ Collects Data ──────────────────── print() ↓ Displays Data
If the user enters Nani, the output is:
num1 = int(input("Enter first number: ")) num2 = int(input("Enter second number: ")) print(num1 + num2)
If the user enters 10 and 20, the output is:
Enter First Number 10 ↓ int(input()) ↓ num1 = 10 Enter Second Number 20 ↓ int(input()) ↓ num2 = 20 num1 + num2 ↓ 30
While learning data-related programming, input() can be used to receive values such as a file name, database name, or processing date.
file_name = input("Enter file name: ") print("Processing:", file_name)
Enter file name: sales.csv Processing: sales.csv
In real production data pipelines, values are often supplied through configuration files, environment variables, APIs, schedulers, or command-line arguments instead of interactive input().
For Now: Learn input() because it helps you understand how a program can receive data dynamically while it is running.

Mistake 1 ❌ Assume input() returns a number age = input("Age: ") Actually: age is a string by default ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ name = input(Enter your name) Correct ✅ name = input("Enter your name: ") Text prompts need quotes. ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ age = input("Age: ") print(age + 5) Correct ✅ age = int(input("Age: ")) print(age + 5) ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Use int() when the user enters text int("Nani") This causes an error because Nani is not a valid integer.
Need Output? ↓ Use print() Need User Input? ↓ Use input() Need Numeric Input? ↓ int(input()) or float(input())

FunctionPurpose
input()Gets data from the user
print()Displays data or output

items.title: Variables
explanation: A variable is a name used to store a value in a Python program.
Simple Definition: A variable is a named reference that allows you to store and use data.
In Python, you create a variable by writing a name, followed by =, followed by a value.
name = "Nani" ↓ ↓ Variable Value age = 25 ↓ ↓ Variable Value
In Python, = is used to assign a value to a variable.
Read it as: Store 25 in age, not age equals 25 in the mathematical sense.
After creating a variable, you can use its name to access the stored value.
name = "Nani" ↓ Variable stores value ↓ print(name) ↓ Python gets "Nani" ↓ Nani
Variables Can Store Different Types of Data
A variable can store different kinds of values.
name = "Nani" age = 25 salary = 25000.50 is_active = True value = None
Variable Value Type ──────────────────────────── name → String age → Integer salary → Float is_active → Boolean value → None
You will learn these data types in more detail in the next topics.
The value stored in a variable can be changed by assigning a new value.
age = 25 ↓ age stores 25 age = 26 ↓ Previous value replaced ↓ age now stores 26
Important: A variable does not permanently store only one value. You can assign a new value to it later.
You can use the value of one variable while creating another value.
price = 100 quantity = 3 total = price * quantity print(total)
You can use the current value of a variable to calculate and store a new value.
count = 10 ↓ Current value = 10 count = count + 1 ↓ 10 + 1 ↓ New value = 11 ↓ Stored back in count

Variable Names Can ✓ Start with a letter ✓ Start with _ ✓ Contain letters ✓ Contain numbers ✓ Contain _ Variable Names Cannot ✗ Start with a number ✗ Contain spaces ✗ Contain special characters like -, @, ! ✗ Use Python keywords
1name = "Nani" # Invalid user name = "Nani" # Invalid user-name = "Nani" # Invalid class = "Python" # Invalid
For example, user-name is invalid because Python interprets - as the subtraction operator.
Python treats uppercase and lowercase letters as different.
name ≠ Name ≠ NAME Python treats them as three different variable names.
Use clear and meaningful variable names. Python commonly uses snake_case.
Avoid unclear names when a meaningful name makes the code easier to understand.
# Less clear x = 25000 # Better monthly_salary = 25000
Good Practice: Choose variable names that explain what the value represents.
Python allows you to assign values to multiple variables in one line.
You can also assign the same value to multiple variables.
x = y = z = 0 print(x) print(y) print(z)
Variables can store the result of calculations and expressions.
num1 = 10 num2 = 20 result = num1 + num2 print(result)
Variables are heavily used in data engineering to store file paths, database names, dates, configuration values, counts, and other information.
source_file = "sales.csv" target_table = "sales_data" record_count = 1000 print(source_file) print(target_table) print(record_count)

Using meaningful names makes data pipeline code easier to read and maintain.

items.title: Data Types
explanation: Data types tell Python what kind of value is being stored and what operations can be performed on that value.
Simple Definition: A data type defines the kind of data a value represents, such as a number, text, true/false value, or no value.
Different types of data are used differently. For example, numbers can be added, while text can be joined together.
Value ↓ Python identifies its type ↓ Number? → Mathematical operations Text? → String operations Boolean? → True / False logic No value? → None
You can use the built-in type() function to check the type of a value or variable.
Memory Rule: Use type() to check what type of data a value is.
These are the basic data types you should understand first.
An integer is a whole number without a decimal point.
A float is a number containing a decimal point.
Remember: 25 is an int, but 25.0 is a float.
25 ↓ int Whole number ──────────────────── 25.0 ↓ float Decimal number
A string represents text data. Strings are written inside quotes.
You can use either single quotes or double quotes for normal strings.
Without quotes, Python may treat a value as a variable name instead of text.
"Nani" ↓ String / Text ──────────────────── Nani ↓ Python looks for a variable named Nani
A Boolean value represents one of two logical states: True or False.
bool ↓ True or False True → Yes / Condition satisfied False → No / Condition not satisfied
Boolean values are commonly used with conditions and decision-making.
Important: Python Boolean values are written as True and False with capital first letters.
None represents the absence of a value.
result = None ↓ Currently no value Later ↓ result = 100 ↓ Now it has a value
None Is Not the Same as Zero or an Empty String
None ↓ No value 0 ↓ Integer with value zero "" ↓ Empty string It is still a string
These are three different values and represent different concepts.
Python usually determines the data type automatically based on the assigned value.
age = 25 price = 99.99 name = "Nani" is_active = True result = None
25 ↓ Python → int 99.99 ↓ Python → float "Nani" ↓ Python → str True ↓ Python → bool None ↓ Python → NoneType
Python allows a variable to be assigned a value of a different type later.
Important: The same variable name can later refer to a value with a different data type.
name = "Nani" age = 25 salary = 25000.50 is_employee = True manager = None print(name) print(age) print(salary) print(is_employee) print(manager)

items.title: Type Conversion
explanation: Type conversion means changing a value from one data type to another.
Simple Definition: Type conversion is the process of converting data from one type to another, such as converting text into a number or a number into text.
Sometimes data comes in a type that is not suitable for the operation you want to perform.
Here, age looks like a number, but because it is inside quotes, it is a string.
If you want to perform mathematical operations, you may need to convert it into an integer.
"25" ↓ str Text Type Conversion ↓ 25 ↓ int Number
The int() function converts a compatible value into an integer.
You can also convert a float into an integer.
Important: Converting a float using int() removes the decimal part. It does not round the value.
25.9 ↓ int(25.9) ↓ 25 Decimal part removed Not rounded
The float() function converts a compatible value into a decimal number.
You can also convert an integer into a float.
The str() function converts a value into a string.
This is useful when combining numbers with text.
age = 25 message = "My age is " + str(age) print(message)
Why Conversion Is Needed When Joining Strings
The following code causes an error because Python cannot directly join a string and an integer using +.
"My age is " ↓ str + 25 ↓ int ❌ Different types cannot be joined this way
Convert the number into a string first.
age = 25 message = "My age is " + str(age) print(message)
The bool() function converts values into either True or False.
Some values are generally treated as False, while many other values are treated as True.
Remember: An empty string, zero, and None are converted to False by bool().
When you manually use functions such as int(), float(), or str(), it is called explicit type conversion.
"100" ↓ str You explicitly use int() ↓ 100 ↓ int
Sometimes Python automatically converts one type into another during an operation. This is called implicit type conversion.
number1 = 10 number2 = 5.5 result = number1 + number2 print(result) print(type(result))
10 ↓ int + 5.5 ↓ float Python automatically handles conversion ↓ 15.5 ↓ float
Type conversion only works when the original value is compatible with the target type.
This works because "25" represents a valid integer.
This causes an error because "Hello" cannot be converted into an integer.
Important: Before converting data, make sure the value is in a format that can be converted to the target data type.
Values received from input() are strings. If you need a number, convert the input.
Even if the user enters 25, the value is received as a string.
User enters 25 ↓ input() ↓ "25" → str ↓ int() ↓ 25 → int
Data from files, APIs, databases, and external systems may not always arrive in the data type you expect.
You may need to convert the values before processing them.
record_count = int(record_count) file_size = float(file_size) source_name = str(source_name)
External Data "1000" ↓ Convert using int() ↓ 1000 ──────────────────── "25.75" ↓ Convert using float() ↓ 25.75 ──────────────────── 123 ↓ Convert using str() ↓ "123"
Correct type conversion is important when cleaning and preparing data for further processing.
Data Engineering Tip: Always check the data type before performing calculations or transformations. Data that looks like a number may actually be stored as text.

Final Definition: Type conversion is the process of changing a value from one data type to another. Python provides functions such as int(), float(), str(), and bool() for explicit conversion, while some conversions happen automatically during operations.

items.title: Python Syntax Basics
explanation: Python syntax is the set of rules that defines how Python code must be written so that the Python interpreter can understand and execute it.
Simple Definition: Python syntax is the correct structure and format used to write Python code.
Python follows specific rules. If the code does not follow those rules, Python may raise a SyntaxError.
This has incorrect syntax because the closing parenthesis is missing.
You write Python code ↓ Python checks the syntax ↓ Correct syntax? ── Yes → Execute code │ No ↓ SyntaxError
Python treats uppercase and lowercase letters as different.
Important: name, Name, and NAME are three different identifiers in Python.
name ↓ Different variable Name ↓ Different variable NAME ↓ Different variable
Python uses indentation to define blocks of code. Indentation means adding spaces at the beginning of a line.
The indented print() statement belongs to the if block.
if age >= 18: ↓ Starts a code block ↓ print("Adult") ↑ Indentation shows this line belongs to the if block
Memory Rule: In Python, indentation is not just for readability. It is part of the syntax.
The standard practice is to use 4 spaces for each level of indentation.
if True: print("Level 1") if True: print("Level 2")
if True: ↓ 4 spaces → Level 1 block if True: ↓ 8 spaces → Level 2 block
Python Uses New Lines to Separate Statements
Normally, each Python statement is written on a separate line.
Statement 1 ↓ name = "Nani" Statement 2 ↓ age = 25 Statement 3 ↓ print(name)
Writing code on separate lines makes it easier to read and maintain.
A colon is used after statements that begin a block, such as if, for, while, def, and class.
if condition: ↑ Colon ↓ Python expects an indented block next
The colon tells Python that a code block follows.
Opening and closing symbols must match correctly.
Important: Every opening parenthesis, bracket, brace, or quote should have the correct closing symbol.
Python ignores some extra spaces, but writing readable code is important.
# Harder to read result=10+20 # Easier to read result = 10 + 20
Both may work, but the second version is easier to understand.
Readable Code variable = value result = number1 + number2 ↓ Easier to understand Easier to debug Easier to maintain
Text after # is treated as a comment and is ignored by the Python interpreter.
# Store the user's age age = 25 print(age)
The comment helps humans understand the code but does not affect program execution.
Python Keywords Cannot Be Used as Variable Names
Python has reserved words called keywords. They have special meanings in the language.
This is invalid because if is a Python keyword.
if else elif for while def class True False None import return
Remember: Do not use Python keywords as variable names.
Variable names, function names, and other names in Python are called identifiers.
Can contain: Letters → a-z, A-Z Numbers → 0-9 Underscore → _ Cannot: Start with a number Contain spaces Contain invalid special characters Use Python keywords

IdentifierValid?Reason
nameYesValid name
user_ageYesUnderscore is allowed
age2YesNumbers allowed after first character
2ageNoCannot start with a number
user ageNoSpaces are not allowed

A code block is a group of statements that belong together. In Python, indentation defines the block.
score = 80 if score >= 50: print("Passed") print("Good job") print("Program finished")
if score >= 50: ↓ print("Passed") print("Good job") ↑ These lines belong to the same block print("Program finished") ↓ Outside the if block
Python syntax focuses strongly on readability. Clear indentation, simple structure, and readable code are important parts of writing Python.
record_count = 100 if record_count > 0: print("Records available") else: print("No records available")
The structure makes it easier to understand the program flow.
Python syntax becomes important when writing scripts and data pipelines. Incorrect indentation or syntax can cause a pipeline to fail.
record_count = 1000 if record_count > 0: print("Starting data processing") print("Records:", record_count) print("Pipeline completed")
Python Script ↓ Check Syntax ↓ Correct indentation? ↓ Execute processing logic ↓ Data pipeline runs
Data Engineering Tip: Syntax errors can stop an entire script or pipeline before processing begins. Writing clean and properly indented code makes debugging easier.

items.title: Operators
explanation: Operators are special symbols or keywords used to perform operations on values and variables.
Simple Definition: Operators tell Python what operation to perform on one or more values.
Here, + is an operator. It tells Python to add a and b.

Operator TypePurpose
ArithmeticPerform mathematical operations
ComparisonCompare two values
LogicalCombine conditions
AssignmentAssign or update values
MembershipCheck whether a value exists in a collection
IdentityCheck whether two references point to the same object
Python Operators │ ├── Arithmetic ├── Comparison ├── Logical ├── Assignment ├── Membership └── Identity
Arithmetic operators are used for mathematical calculations.
a = 10 b = 3 print(a + b) print(a - b) print(a * b) print(a / b) print(a // b) print(a % b) print(a ** b)
Floor division returns the whole-number part of the division result.
The modulus operator returns the remainder after division.
Common Use: The modulus operator is useful for checking whether a number is even or odd.
Comparison operators compare two values and return either True or False.

OperatorMeaningExample
==Equal to10 == 10 → True
!=Not equal to10 != 5 → True
>Greater than10 > 5 → True
<Less than10 < 5 → False
>=Greater than or equal to10 >= 10 → True
<=Less than or equal to5 <= 10 → True
a = 10 b = 5 print(a == b) print(a != b) print(a > b) print(a < b) print(a >= b) print(a <= b)
Important: = assigns a value, while == compares two values.
= → Store a value age = 25 == → Compare values age == 25 ↓ True
Logical operators are used to combine or reverse conditions.

OperatorMeaning
andTrue when both conditions are True
orTrue when at least one condition is True
notReverses a boolean value
age = 25 has_id = True print(age >= 18 and has_id)
Condition 1: age >= 18 → True Condition 2: has_id → True True AND True ↓ True
is_admin = False is_manager = True print(is_admin or is_manager)
False OR True ↓ True Only one condition needs to be True.
not True ↓ False not False ↓ True
Assignment operators are used to assign or update values in variables.

OperatorExampleEquivalent To
=x = 10Assign 10 to x
+=x += 5x = x + 5
-=x -= 5x = x - 5
*=x *= 5x = x * 5
/=x /= 5x = x / 5
//=x //= 5x = x // 5
%=x %= 5x = x % 5
**=x **= 2x = x ** 2
Membership operators check whether a value exists inside a collection such as a string, list, tuple, set, or dictionary.

OperatorMeaning
inReturns True if the value exists
not inReturns True if the value does not exist
languages = ["Python", "SQL", "Java"] print("Python" in languages) print("C++" in languages)
languages ↓ [Python, SQL, Java] "Python" in languages ↓ True "C++" in languages ↓ False
Data Engineering Use: Membership operators are useful when checking whether expected columns, values, or records exist in data.
columns = ["id", "name", "salary"] if "salary" in columns: print("Column exists")
Identity operators check whether two variables refer to the same object in memory.

OperatorMeaning
isTrue if both references point to the same object
is notTrue if both references do not point to the same object
Important: Use == to compare values. Use is when checking object identity. A common example is checking x is None.
== checks whether the values are equal.
Operators are frequently used when processing, validating, and transforming data.

record_count = 100 failed_records = 5 success_records = record_count - failed_records if success_records > 0: print("Data processed") if failed_records == 0: print("No failures") else: print("Some records failed")

items.title: Truthy and Falsy Values
explanation: In Python, every value can be treated as either True or False when Python evaluates it in a condition.
Simple Definition: A truthy value behaves like True, while a falsy value behaves like False in a condition.
Since the string "Python" is non-empty, Python treats it as True.
value = "Python" ↓ Non-empty string ↓ Truthy ↓ Condition is treated as True
A truthy value is not necessarily equal to the Boolean value True. It simply behaves as True when Python checks it in a Boolean context.
A falsy value behaves as False when Python evaluates it in a Boolean context.
The following commonly used values are treated as falsy in Python.
Common Falsy Values │ ├── False ├── None ├── 0 ├── 0.0 ├── "" ├── [] ├── {} ├── () └── set()
Generally, non-empty collections, non-empty strings, and non-zero numbers are truthy.
Easy Rule: Empty values and zero are usually falsy. Non-empty values and non-zero numbers are usually truthy.
The bool() function converts a value into its Boolean representation.
Python automatically checks the truthiness of a value inside an if statement.
name = "Nani" if name: print("Name is available")
Because name contains a non-empty string, the condition is truthy.
name = "" if name: print("Name is available") else: print("Name is empty")
if value: ↓ Python checks bool(value) ↓ True? → Run if block False? → Skip if block
You can directly check whether a list contains values.
records = [] if records: print("Records available") else: print("No records found")
records = [] ↓ Empty list ↓ Falsy ↓ else block runs
file_name = "data.csv" if file_name: print("File name available")
file_name = "" if not file_name: print("File name is missing")
file_name = "" ↓ Falsy → False ↓ not False ↓ True ↓ if block runs
None represents the absence of a value and is falsy.
result = None if result: print("Result available") else: print("No result available")
Important: Although None is falsy, use is None when you specifically want to check whether a value is None.
result = None if result is None: print("No result available")
Truthy and falsy values are also important when using and, or, and not.
name = "Nani" age = 25 if name and age: print("Both values are available")
Both values are truthy, so the condition runs.
name = "" age = 25 if name or age: print("At least one value is available")

ConceptMeaning
FalseThe actual Boolean value False
FalsyAny value that behaves like False in a Boolean context
Both False and 0 are falsy, but they are different concepts.
Falsy Values │ ├── False ├── 0 ├── "" ├── [] ├── {} └── None All behave as False in a Boolean context
Truthy and falsy values are useful when checking whether data is available before processing it.
records = [ {"id": 1, "name": "Nani"}, {"id": 2, "name": "Kumar"} ] if records: print("Starting data processing") else: print("No records to process")
Data Source ↓ records ↓ Check: if records ↓ Non-empty? ── Yes → Process data │ No ↓ No records to process
You may also use truthy and falsy checks when validating simple values.
file_path = "" if not file_path: print("File path is required")
file_path = "" ↓ Falsy ↓ not file_path ↓ True ↓ Show missing value message
Data Engineering Tip: Before processing data, it is common to check whether a collection or input contains values. For example, if records: checks whether the collection is non-empty.

Mistake 1 ❌ Assuming only False is falsy Falsy values also include: 0, "", [], {}, (), None ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Checking a list unnecessarily if len(records) > 0: Often simpler: if records: ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Using == None Less preferred: if value == None: Preferred: if value is None: ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Assuming 0 means None 0 is falsy, but it is still a valid number.
Truthy ↓ Usually non-empty or non-zero Examples: 1 "Python" [1, 2] {"id": 1} ──────────────── Falsy ↓ Usually empty, zero, False, or None Examples: False None 0 "" [] {} () set()

ConceptKey Point
TruthyBehaves like True in a Boolean context
FalsyBehaves like False in a Boolean context
bool()Converts a value to True or False
Non-empty stringTruthy
Empty stringFalsy
Non-zero numberTruthy
ZeroFalsy
Non-empty collectionTruthy
Empty collectionFalsy
NoneFalsy

Final Definition: Truthy and falsy values describe how Python treats values in Boolean contexts. Non-empty and non-zero values are generally truthy, while False, None, zero, and empty collections are commonly falsy.
practice: Step 1: Use bool() to check different values.

Step 2: Check empty and non-empty collections.

Step 3: Use a truthy value in an if statement.

Step 4: Check an empty list.

Step 5: Check a missing string value using not.
file_name = "" if not file_name: print("File name is required")
Step 6: Check whether a value is specifically None.
result = None if result is None: print("Result is None")
Step 7: Create a simple data processing check.
records = [101, 102, 103] if records: print("Processing", len(records), "records") else: print("No records available")

items.title: Conditional Statements
explanation: Conditional statements allow a Python program to make decisions and execute different code depending on whether a condition is True or False.
Simple Definition: Conditional statements are used to control which block of code runs based on a condition.
Condition ↓ True or False? ↓ True → Run selected code False → Skip or run another block
Programs often need to make decisions based on input, data, or a particular situation.
The program checks the condition and decides whether the message should be printed.
Key Idea: Conditions help a program choose what to do next.
The if statement runs a block of code only when its condition is True.
if condition: # code to run when condition is True
What Happens When the if Condition Is False?
If the condition is False, Python skips the code inside the if block.
marks = 40 if marks >= 50: print("Passed") print("Program finished")
marks >= 50? ↓ False ↓ Skip if block ↓ Continue program
Use else when you want one block to run if the condition is True and another block to run if it is False.
if condition: # runs when True else: # runs when False
age = 16 if age >= 18: print("Eligible") else: print("Not eligible")
elif means else if. It allows you to check another condition when the previous condition is False.
if condition1: # code elif condition2: # code else: # code
marks = 75 if marks >= 90: print("Grade A") elif marks >= 60: print("Grade B") else: print("Grade C")
marks = 75 ↓ marks >= 90? → False ↓ marks >= 60? → True ↓ Print "Grade B" ↓ Remaining blocks are skipped
Python checks conditions from top to bottom. Once it finds the first condition that is True, it runs that block and skips the remaining elif and else blocks.
marks = 95 if marks >= 60: print("Passed") elif marks >= 90: print("Excellent")
The first condition is already true, so Python never checks the elif condition.
marks = 95 if marks >= 90: print("Excellent") elif marks >= 60: print("Passed") else: print("Failed")
Important: Place more specific conditions before broader conditions when their ranges overlap.

OperatorMeaningExample
==Equal toa == b
!=Not equal toa != b
>Greater thana > b
<Less thana < b
>=Greater than or equal toa >= b
<=Less than or equal toa <= b
You can combine multiple conditions using logical operators.
age = 25 country = "India" if age >= 18 and country == "India": print("Condition matched")
The result is true only when both conditions are true.
if age >= 18 and age <= 60: print("Working age")
The result is true when at least one condition is true.
day = "Sunday" if day == "Saturday" or day == "Sunday": print("Weekend")
is_active = False if not is_active: print("Account is inactive")
Python conditions do not always need comparison operators. Python can directly evaluate whether a value is truthy or falsy.
name = "Nani" if name: print("Name is available")
A non-empty string is truthy, so the if block runs.
records = [] if records: print("Records available") else: print("No records found")
Remember: Empty strings, empty collections, 0, False, and None are commonly treated as falsy.
A nested conditional statement is an if statement inside another conditional block.
age = 25 has_id = True if age >= 18: if has_id: print("Access allowed") else: print("ID required") else: print("Underage")
age >= 18? ↓ True ↓ has_id? ┌──True──→ Access allowed │ False ↓ ID required
Nested conditions are useful, but avoid making code unnecessarily deep when a simpler condition can be used.
Conditional statements are commonly used to validate data before processing it.
records = [101, 102, 103] if records: print("Starting data processing") else: print("No records to process")
Data Source ↓ Records received? ↓ ┌──Yes──→ Process records │ No ↓ No records to process
age = None if age is None: print("Age is missing") elif age < 0: print("Invalid age") else: print("Valid age")
Data Engineering Use: Conditions are useful for checking missing values, validating data, handling errors, and deciding how data should be processed.

Mistake 1 ❌ Using = instead of == if age = 18: Correct: if age == 18: ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Forgetting the colon if age >= 18 Correct: if age >= 18: ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Incorrect indentation if age >= 18: print("Eligible") Correct: if age >= 18: print("Eligible") ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Incorrect condition order if marks >= 60: print("Passed") elif marks >= 90: print("Excellent") More specific conditions should come first.
if ↓ Check one condition if + else ↓ Choose between two paths if + elif + else ↓ Choose between multiple paths Python checks ↓ Top to Bottom ↓ First True condition wins

ConceptKey Point
ifRuns code when a condition is True
elseRuns when previous conditions are False
elifChecks another condition
Condition orderPython checks from top to bottom
First True conditionIts block runs and remaining blocks are skipped
andBoth conditions must be True
orAt least one condition must be True
notReverses the Boolean result
IndentationDefines the conditional code block

Final Definition: Conditional statements allow a Python program to make decisions by checking conditions and executing different blocks of code depending on whether those conditions evaluate to True or False.
practice: Step 1: Create a simple if statement.
age = 20 if age >= 18: print("Adult")
Step 2: Use if...else.
number = 7 if number % 2 == 0: print("Even") else: print("Odd")
Step 3: Use if...elif...else.
marks = 75 if marks >= 90: print("A") elif marks >= 60: print("B") else: print("C")
Step 4: Combine conditions using and.
age = 25 if age >= 18 and age <= 60: print("Working age")
Step 5: Combine conditions using or.
day = "Sunday" if day == "Saturday" or day == "Sunday": print("Weekend")
Step 6: Use not to check an empty value.
name = "" if not name: print("Name is required")
Step 7: Validate simple data.
records = [] if records: print("Processing records") else: print("No records available")
Step 8: Check for a missing value.
value = None if value is None: print("Value is missing") else: print("Value is available")
Final Understanding Check:

1. What is a conditional statement? 2. What is the difference between if, elif, and else? 3. What happens when an if condition is False? 4. In what order does Python check conditions? 5. What happens after Python finds the first True condition? 6. Why is condition order important? 7. What is the difference between == and =? 8. What does and mean in a condition? 9. What does or mean in a condition? 10. What does not do? 11. Can a truthy or falsy value be used directly in an if statement? 12. Why is indentation important in conditional statements?
Practice Goal: You should be able to use if, elif, and else, combine conditions with logical operators, understand condition order, and apply conditions for basic data validation.

items.title: Loops
explanation: A loop allows you to execute the same block of code repeatedly.
Simple Definition: A loop is used to repeat a block of code while iterating over data or while a condition remains true.
Start ↓ Run code ↓ Run code again ↓ Repeat until finished
Without loops, you would need to write the same code repeatedly.
print("Process record") print("Process record") print("Process record")
for i in range(3): print("Process record")
Key Idea: Write the code once and let the loop repeat it.
Python mainly provides two types of loops:
Python Loops │ ├── for loop │ └── Iterate over a sequence or collection │ └── while loop └── Repeat while a condition is True
A for loop is used to iterate through an iterable such as a list, string, tuple, dictionary, or range.
[10, 20, 30] ↓ First item → 10 → Run code Second item → 20 → Run code Third item → 30 → Run code ↓ Finished
for variable in iterable: # code to repeat

PartMeaning
forStarts the loop
variableStores the current item
inConnects the variable with the iterable
iterableThe collection or sequence being iterated
:Starts the loop block
IndentationDefines the code that belongs to the loop
names = ["Nani", "Kumar", "Ravi"] for name in names: print(name)
names ↓ ["Nani", "Kumar", "Ravi"] ↓ name = "Nani" → Run name = "Kumar" → Run name = "Ravi" → Run ↓ Finished
A string can also be iterated character by character.
word = "Python" for letter in word: print(letter)
P y t h o n
range() is commonly used when you want to repeat code a specific number of times.
Important: range(5) starts at 0 and stops before 5.
range(stop) range(start, stop) range(start, stop, step)
Remember: The stop value is not included.
A while loop repeats a block of code as long as its condition is True.
count = 1 ↓ Is count <= 3? ↓ Yes Print count ↓ Increase count ↓ Check condition again ↓ No → Stop
The condition is checked before every iteration.
Key Rule: The loop continues while the condition is True. It stops when the condition becomes False.
In many while loops, you must update a value so that the condition eventually becomes False.
If count += 1 is missing, the loop may run forever.
count = 1 ↓ Condition is True ↓ Run loop ↓ Value updated? ↙ ↘ Yes No ↓ ↓ Eventually May create stop infinite loop
An infinite loop happens when a loop condition never becomes False.
Here, count never changes, so count <= 3 remains true forever.
Warning: Always make sure a while loop has a way to eventually stop.

forwhile
Iterates through an iterableRepeats while a condition is true
Useful for lists, strings, ranges, etc.Useful when repetitions depend on a condition
Usually has a clear end based on itemsMust ensure the condition eventually becomes false
Use for ↓ When iterating over data Examples: List String Dictionary range() ──────────────── Use while ↓ When repeating based on a condition Example: while count <= 10
A nested loop is a loop inside another loop.
for i in range(2): for j in range(3): print(i, j)
For every iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop completes all of its iterations.
Outer Loop: i = 0 ├── j = 0 ├── j = 1 └── j = 2 Outer Loop: i = 1 ├── j = 0 ├── j = 1 └── j = 2
Dictionaries can be iterated in different ways.
student = { "name": "Nani", "age": 25 } for key in student: print(key)
for key, value in student.items(): print(key, value)
Note: Dictionaries will be covered in more detail in the Data Structures section.
Loops are heavily used to process multiple records.
records = [ {"id": 101, "name": "Nani"}, {"id": 102, "name": "Kumar"}, {"id": 103, "name": "Ravi"} ] for record in records: print(record["id"], record["name"])
Data Records ↓ for each record ↓ Read record ↓ Process record ↓ Next record ↓ All records completed
sales = [100, 250, 300, 150] total = 0 for amount in sales: total += amount print(total)

Mistake 1 ❌ Forgetting the colon for i in range(5) Correct: for i in range(5): ──────────────────── Mistake 2 ❌ Incorrect indentation for i in range(3): print(i) Correct: for i in range(3): print(i) ──────────────────── Mistake 3 ❌ Expecting range(5) to include 5 range(5) Gives: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 ──────────────────── Mistake 4 ❌ Creating an infinite while loop while count <= 3: print(count) Update count so the condition can become False.
for loop ↓ Repeat for each item while loop ↓ Repeat while condition is True range() ↓ Generate a sequence of numbers Stop value ↓ Usually not included

LoopRepeats a block of code
forIterates through items
whileRepeats while a condition is True
range()Generates a sequence of numbers

Nested loopA loop inside another loop

Final Definition: Loops allow Python to repeatedly execute code. Use for when iterating through data and while when repetition depends on a condition.

items.title: `break`, `continue`, `pass`
explanation: break, continue, and pass are Python statements used to control how code executes, especially inside loops and conditional blocks.
Simple Definition: break stops a loop, continue skips the current iteration, and pass does nothing and acts as a placeholder.
Loop or Code Block ↓ ┌──────┼──────┐ ↓ ↓ ↓ break continue pass ↓ ↓ ↓ Stop Skip Do nothing loop current placeholder iteration
The break statement immediately stops the nearest loop. After break runs, Python exits the loop and continues with the code after it.
for number in range(1, 6): if number == 4: break print(number) print("Loop finished")
number = 1 → Print number = 2 → Print number = 3 → Print number = 4 → break ↓ Exit loop
When number becomes 4, the condition is true. Python executes break, so the loop stops immediately.
count = 1 while True: print(count) if count == 3: break count += 1
while True creates a loop that would normally continue forever. The break statement provides the condition for exiting it.
Key Point: break exits the entire nearest loop, not just the current iteration.
Real Example: Stop When Data Is Found ⭐
records = [101, 102, 103, 104] for record in records: if record == 103: print("Record found") break
Once the required record is found, there may be no need to continue searching.
The continue statement skips the remaining code in the current iteration and moves to the next iteration of the loop.
for number in range(1, 6): if number == 3: continue print(number)
number = 1 → Print number = 2 → Print number = 3 → continue ↓ Skip remaining code ↓ Next iteration number = 4 → Print number = 5 → Print
When number is 3, Python does not execute print(number). It immediately starts the next iteration.
values = [10, None, 20, None, 30] for value in values: if value is None: continue print(value)
Read value ↓ Is value None? ┌──Yes──→ continue → Skip processing │ No ↓ Process value
This pattern is useful when processing data and you want to skip invalid, missing, or unwanted records.
Key Point: continue does not stop the loop. It only skips the current iteration.
The pass statement does nothing. It is used when Python requires a statement, but you do not want to write the actual code yet.
Without pass, an empty code block would cause a syntax error.
The function is created successfully, but it currently has no implementation.
for number in range(1, 4): if number == 2: pass print(number)
Unlike break or continue, pass does not change the flow of the loop. Python simply continues normally.
Key Point: pass means: "Do nothing here for now."

StatementWhat It DoesLoop Continues?
breakImmediately exits the loopNo
continueSkips the current iterationYes
passDoes nothingYes, normally

break Iteration ↓ Condition? ↓ Yes STOP ENTIRE LOOP ────────────────── continue Iteration ↓ Condition? ↓ Yes SKIP CURRENT ITERATION ↓ NEXT ITERATION ────────────────── pass Code Block ↓ pass ↓ DO NOTHING ↓ CONTINUE NORMALLY
# break for number in range(1, 6): if number == 3: break print(number)
# continue for number in range(1, 6): if number == 3: continue print(number)
Easy Memory Rule: break = Stop. continue = Skip. pass = Nothing.
A break statement exits only the nearest loop containing it.
for i in range(1, 3): for j in range(1, 4): if j == 2: break print(i, j)
When j == 2, only the inner loop stops. The outer loop continues.
These statements can be useful when processing many records.
records = [100, None, 200, -1, 300] for record in records: if record is None: continue if record == -1: print("Stop signal received") break print("Processing:", record)
